title: Colorado OAC Workers' Compensation Decision — WC 5-302-636-001
text:
Office of Administrative Courts
State of Colorado
Workers’ Compensation No. WC 5-302-636-001
Issues
Whether Claimant proved by a preponderance of the evidence that she sustained
⮚
a compensable industrial injury on April 8, 2025.
Whether Claimant proved by a preponderance of the evidence that she is entitled
⮚
to reasonable, necessary and causally related medical benefits, including the
reverse total right shoulder arthroplasty performed by Jon-Michael Caldwell, MD
on July 3, 2025.
Stipulations
At hearing the parties stipulated that, if the claim is found compensable,
Claimant’s average weekly wage (AWW) is $752.77 and Claimant is entitled to
temporary total disability (TTD) benefits April 9, 2025, ongoing.
Findings of Fact
1. Claimant is 68 years old. Claimant worked for Employer for approximately 20
years as a driver technician. Claimant’s job duties involved driving a flatbed truck
to deliver items. Claimant was required to strap down the load of items on the
back of the truck.
2. Claimant has a history of prior right shoulder pain for which she treated with
William Ciccone, MD at Orthopedic Centers of Colorado. On July 2, 2021,
Claimant presented to Dr. Ciccone with complaints of right shoulder pain that had
been presented for about two years. Claimant denied any specific injuries.
Claimant complained of pain mostly over the anterior aspect of the shoulder,
worsened at night, and with reaching and lifting. X-rays demonstrated mild
degenerative changes. Dr. Ciccone diagnosed Claimant with right shoulder pain
1

and recommended a course of physical therapy and a diagnostic ultrasound to
evaluate possible rotator cuff pathology. Claimant did not undergo physical
therapy.
3. Claimant returned to Dr. Ciccone on November 18, 2022 for continued evaluation
of her right shoulder pain. Dr. Ciccone noted that Claimant underwent shoulder
injections in the past that were quite helpful. Claimant again reported pain with
reaching and lifting without any specific injury. Dr. Ciccone diagnosed right
shoulder pain with degenerative changes, performed a steroid injection, and
prescribed Claimant Mobic.
4. On July 5, 2024, Claimant again presented to Dr. Ciccone for right shoulder
complaints. Dr. Ciccone noted that the onset of symptoms was gradual and
occurred during recreational activities. Claimant reported worsening symptoms
with an aching, burning and sharp pain that interfered with her sleep. Claimant
further reported pain mostly overly the anterolateral aspect of the shoulder, and
pain with reaching and lifting. X-rays demonstrated significant degenerative
changes in the glenohumeral joint. Dr. Ciccone diagnosed Claimant with right
shoulder pain with glenohumeral arthritis. Dr. Ciccone administered another
steroid injection. Claimant was to follow-up with any persistent complaints.
5. During a regular work shift on April 8, 2025, Claimant experienced a pop in her
right shoulder and felt an immediate onset of pain while throwing a strap over a
load of lumbar on the flat bed of her truck. Claimant reported to her supervisor,
John Gunzer, that she was in pain. Mr. Gunzer released Claimant from work for
the remainder of the day and Claimant went home. Claimant returned to work the
next day with continued pain. Claimant performed one delivery and was unable
to complete her work shift due to the pain.
6. On April 9, 2025, Claimant presented to Sharon Walker, MD at Colorado
Occupational Medical Partners. Claimant completed intake paperwork in which
she reported that the injury occurred when she “Was strapping down material on
flat bed throug [sic] straps over load heard something pop & and [sic] tightened
2

load to head back to yard.” CHE 7, p. 43. Claimant reported to Dr. Walker that
she was at work the day prior throwing a strap over a load on the back of a truck
and experienced immediate significant right shoulder pain. Claimant reported that
her right shoulder started aching on April 4, 2025, but it got much worse
yesterday. Claimant reported 8/10 shoulder pain radiating into her neck and
upper back. Dr. Walker found Claimant’s exam consistent with an anterior
shoulder dislocation and attempted to relocate Claimant’s right shoulder. Due to
the pain, Dr. Walker stopped her attempt and directed Claimant to the
emergency room. Dr. Walker removed Claimant from work.
7. That same day Claimant presented to the emergency department at HCA
HealthOne Swedish Hospital with complaints of right shoulder anterior pain. The
provider noted a history of arthritis. Claimant reported that she was throwing
straps over the load in her flatbed to secure the load when she felt her shoulder
pop out of place. X-rays of the right shoulder demonstrated severe glenohumeral
and AC joint osteoarthritis with no fracture or dislocation. The provider suspected
a shoulder strain and recommended Claimant treat with Tylenol, heat and ice.
8. Claimant returned to Dr. Walker on April 10, 2025 with complaints of 7-9/10
shoulder pain. On exam, Dr. Walker noted a very large purple, green and yellow
ecchymosis on the center of Claimant’s chest approximately 12 centimeters in
diameter. Dr. Walker noted she did not see the bruise the day prior because it
was covered by Claimant’s shirt. Claimant reported that the bruise happened last
week. Dr. Walker further noted a small dark purple bruise about 2 centimeters in
diameter on the right lateral chest that Claimant reported was new. Dr. Walker
ordered an MRI of the right shoulder, which revealed:
1. There is severe glenohumeral joint arthritis with edema.
2. Multiple subchondral cysts.
3. There is diffuse tearing of the inferior anterior, superior and posterior
superior labrum.
3

4. There is severe synovial thickening in the joint. This may be seen with a
chronic inflammatory arthritis and could be seen with rheumatoid
arthritis or a seronegative arthritis.
5. There is a large extensive subacromial subdeltoid bursal effusion.
6. There is a full-thickness tear of the supraspinatus tendon.
7. There is severe supraspinatus and subscapularis, moderate teres minor
and mild infraspinatus muscle atrophy.
8. There is a large loose body in the subcoracoid bursa consistent with a
synovial osteochondroma. There is also a large loose body along the
superior aspect of the supraspinatus muscle.
RHE F, pp. 77-78.
9. Dr. Walker noted that the MRI findings were all chronic changes. She diagnosed
Claimant with a right shoulder sprain, effusion, reactive arthritis and arm
paresthesia. Dr. Walker noted that the objective findings were consistent with
history and/or work-related mechanism of injury. Dr. Walker referred Claimant for
physical therapy and released Claimant to modified duty with restrictions of
wearing a sling and no use of the right arm or driving of the company vehicle.
10.On April 29, 2025, Claimant saw Monica Fanning Schubert, NP under the
supervision of Matthew Lugliani, MD at Colorado Occupational Medicine
Partners. Claimant was overall about the same. NP Schubert continued
Claimant’s work restrictions. NP Schubert noted that the objective findings were
consistent with history and/or work-related mechanism of injury.
11.On April 10, 2025, Employer filed a First Report of Injury stating that the injury
occurred while Claimant was using a winch bar that ratchets the strap tighter.
12.Insurer filed a Notice of Contest on May 1, 2025.
13.On May 5, 2025, conducted a Job Demands Analysis for the
position of delivery driver at Employer. The analysis determined that the position
required light to medium physical demands. It was noted that while the job
4

involves throwing and tightening straps, the specific frequency and force
standards for cumulative trauma risk factors were not met during the observation.
14.On May 7, 2025, Claimant attended a physical therapy session with Robert
Rapier, PT. PT Rapier noted high levels of deficits in motion and strength. PT
Rapier noted that Claimant’s return to work might be in a limited capacity given
the results of her MRI and extensive degenerative joint disease of the shoulder.
15.Claimant attended physical therapy appointments on May 9, May 13, May 16,
and May 23, 2025, reporting improvement in her pain and function.
16.At a follow-up appointment with NP Schubert on May 13, 2025, Claimant
reported that physical therapy was helping to a mild degree, with improved range
of motion but continued pain and disrupted sleep. NP Schubert referred Claimant
for an orthopedic evaluation to address Claimant’s “acute flare-up of chronic
degenerative condition.” CHE 7, p. 62. Claimant continued under work
restrictions of minimal use of the right arm, wearing the sling as needed, and no
driving the company vehicle.
17.On May 29, 2025, PT Rapier noted that Claimant reported feeling much better
with minimal problems and felt ready to go back to work. Claimant was noted to
lift up to 25 pounds in physical therapy with no issues at that time.
18.On May 30, 2025, Claimant reported to NP Schubert better range of motion but
continued pain with raising her arm overhead or with internal rotation. Claimant
reported that she thought she could do okay returning to driving but was
concerned with throwing the straps to secure the loads. Claimant was released to
modified duty with the following restrictions: 10 pounds maximum lifting/repetitive
lifting/carrying/pushing/pulling on the right, and no reaching overhead or driving
the company vehicle.
19.On June 3, 2025, Claimant saw orthopedic surgeon Jon-Michael Etienne
Caldwell, MD at Panorama Orthopedics & Spine Center. Claimant reported
experiencing a sharp onset of new shoulder pain while throwing a strap over the
5

top of the load on a flatbed. Claimant reported feeling a pop in her shoulder at
the time and with significantly worsened shoulder pain and functional disability
since. Dr. Caldwell noted, “Prior to this injury, she did have about 2 months of
aching in the shoulder however the symptoms did not reach the level where she
felt she required any treatment.” CHE 9, p. 106. Dr. Caldwell noted that physical
exam and imaging were consistent with severe glenohumeral osteoarthritis, a full
thickness rotator cuff tear, extensive subacromial and subdeltoid effusion, and
varying degrees of atrophy involving her entire rotator cuff. He remarked, “While
the imaging findings show pathology which is certainly chronic, she reports she
was minimally symptomatic prior to her recent workplace injury on April 8.
Therefore it is reasonable to conclude this injury is responsible for acutely
exacerbating the symptoms of her chronic underlying condition.” Id. at 105. Dr.
Caldwell diagnosed Claimant with right shoulder rotator cuff arthropathy. He
noted that Claimant had undergone conservative treatment without significant
improvement and, given the severity of her imaging findings, it was unlikely any
conservative treatment would provide durable relief. Dr. Caldwell recommended
Claimant undergo a reverse total shoulder arthroplasty.
20.On June 4, 2025, PT Rapier noted that Claimant was more hesitant after seeing
the surgeon and was not sure if going back to work was the right thing to do.
21.On June 9, 2025, Albert Hattem, MD performed a utilization review for
Respondents. Dr. Hattem opined that Claimant’s right shoulder condition and the
recommended surgery were not work-related. Dr. Hattem concluded that the MRI
demonstrated only pre-existing changes with no evidence of acute injury. He
opined that the reported mechanism of injury of tossing a strap over a load on a
flatbed was only an insignificant minor stress on the shoulder and unlikely to
exacerbate or significantly aggravate Claimant’s very significant pre-existing
degenerative condition. He further opined that there was no repetitive-type right
shoulder injury based on the job demands analysis. Dr. Hattem noted that
Claimant had been experiencing a right shoulder ache for two months prior to the
6

work incident. Dr. Hattem further opined that the large bruise Claimant’s chest
indicated that there was a non-work-related traumatic event that was more likely
to aggravate her pre-existing right shoulder degenerative condition.
22.NP Schubert continued Claimant’s work restrictions at a follow-up appointment
on June 10, 2025. Claimant reported 7/10 pain and felt she could do her regular
job because of the shoulder function and pain.
23.On July 3, 2025, Claimant underwent a right reverse total shoulder arthroplasty
performed by Dr. Caldwell under her private insurance.
24.Claimant attended multiple postoperative appointments with Dr. Caldwell. As of
November 5, 2025, he noted that Claimant was recovering well and was able to
return to work with a 30-pound lifting restriction, 10-pound overhead lifting
restriction, and should avoid repetitive overhead lifting, sudden jerking, or high
impact forces.
25.On February 11, 2026, Melissa Koenig, MD performed an Independent Medical
Examination (IME) at the request of Respondents. Dr. Koenig noted that
Claimant described the mechanism of injury to her as releasing the straps used
to secure the load, which contrasted with Claimant’s prior reports where she
stated she was throwing straps across the load and felt a pop in her shoulder. Dr.
Koening opined that Claimant did not sustain a work-related right shoulder injury.
Dr. Koenig noted that Claimant had a several-month history of prior right
shoulder pain and acknowledged during the IME that she had prior right shoulder
treatment for arthritis including injections. Dr. Koenig opined that the MRI findings
were chronic and agreed with Dr. Hattem that tossing a strap over a load on a
flatbed would be considered a minor stress on the shoulder not likely to
exacerbate or significantly aggravate the pre-existing degenerative condition.
She further opined that it was reasonable to expect that some sort of traumatic
event caused the large bruise was more likely to aggravate Claimant’s pre-
existing right shoulder arthritis. Dr. Koenig concluded that, while Claimant had a
pre-existing condition of rotator cuff tear arthropathy, this condition was not
7

permanently aggravated or accelerated on April 8, 2025. Dr. Koening noted that
physical therapy records documented Claimant’s improvement and ability to
return to work until seeing Dr. Caldwell. She opined that the right reverse total
shoulder replacement was appropriate but not necessary as Claimant had
functional improvement with conservative treatment and no injection was
attempted.
26.Claimant credibly testified at hearing. Claimant testified that, prior to the work
incident, she did experience aches and pains in her right shoulder but the
symptoms did not require consistent treatment nor cause her to miss any time
from work. Claimant testified that, prior to April 2025, she underwent
approximately three steroid injections to her right shoulder over the course of
approximately five years. Claimant testified that, on April 8 2025, she heard a
pop while throwing a strap over the load in the flatbed, she felt immediate pain
and her arm became “lame.” Claimant testified that she had never felt this pain
prior to April 8, 2025 and that the pain was different from her prior pain. Claimant
testified she was unaware of how she sustained the bruise on her chest, and that
it could have been from lifting or carrying something while performing her job
duties. Claimant testified that she has not been able to return to work due to her
injury. Claimant testified that, prior to undergoing surgery, she was not back to
her baseline in terms of pain or function. Claimant testified that, prior to the work
injury, she was able to raise her arm overhead, but could not raise it very high.
She testified that, after the injury but prior to the surgery, she was unable to raise
her arm overhead or to the side. Claimant testified that after the injury she
experienced decreased strength, range of motion, and lifting ability. She testified
that the surgery resulted in decreased pain and symptoms and improved
function.
27.Employer’s owner and president, John Gunzer, credibly testified at hearing on
behalf of Employer. Mr. Gunzer testified that Claimant came directly to him on
April 8, 2025 reporting that she was in too much pain and needed to go home.
8

Mr. Gunzer testified that his understanding at that time was that Claimant was
not reporting a work injury. Mr. Gunzer testified that Claimant returned to work on
April 9, 2025 with continued reports of pain and was then taken to urgent care.
Mr. Gunzer testified that Claimant had previously taken a lot of time off of work
for various things, but specifically only referenced one day as related to
Claimant’s right shoulder for a shoulder injection appointment. Mr. Gunzner
testified that prior to April 8, 2025, Claimant was working her full duty job without
restrictions or limitations. He testified that following her work incident, Claimant
would continually come into work to give medical reports and indicate work
restrictions and ask about light duty work. Mr. Gunzer testified that Claimant has
not returned to work for Employer, as she has not yet been released for available
work.
28.Dr. Koening testified at hearing on behalf of Respondents as a Level II accredited
expert in orthopedic surgery. Dr. Koening testified consistent with her IME report.
Dr. Koenig testified that Claimant told her she was injured releasing, not
throwing, the straps, and that Claimant did not mention anything about her
shoulder being dislocated. Dr. Koenig testified that neither reported mechanism
of injury was sufficient to cause Claimant’s injury or symptoms. Dr. Koenig
testified that people, especially those over the age of 60, can have a tear in their
shoulders without even knowing it. Dr. Koenig testified there is no way to
determine whether the swelling shown on Claimant’s imaging was a result of her
chronic condition or an acute injury. Dr. Koenig testified that Dr. Ciccone’s
records reinforce her opinion that Claimant had a significant pre-existing
condition. She testified that Claimant’s presentation is typical of arthritis. Dr.
Koenig testified the reverse total surgery was reasonable, but not necessary or
related to the work incident. Dr. Koenig testified that an injection would have
been the next reasonable step, and that Claimant was basically back to baseline
before the surgery occurred.
9

29.The ALJ finds the testimony of Claimant and the opinions of Dr. Walker, Dr.
Caldwell and NP Schubert, as corroborated by the records, more credible and
persuasive than the testimony of Mr. Gunzer and the opinions of Drs. Hattem and
Koenig. The ALJ does not find Drs. Hattem and Koenig’s attribution of Claimant’s
injury to a totally speculative, unknown event based on a bruise persuasive.
Additionally, the records indicate that Claimant was forthcoming about, and her
providers considered, her symptoms leading up to the work injury, as
documented by Drs. Walker and Caldwell, as well as NP Schubert.
30.Claimant proved it is more probably true than not she suffered a compensable
industrial injury arising out of and in the scope of her employment on April 8,
2025. Claimant’s employment on April 8, 2025 aggravated Claimant’s pre-
existing chronic condition producing a disability and need for medical treatment.
31.Claimant proved it is more probably true than not the treatment she received for
her right shoulder, including the reverse right total shoulder arthroplasty, was
reasonable, necessary, and related treatment to cure and relieve the effects of
her April 8, 2025 industrial injury. Claimant is entitled to reasonably necessary
medical treatment related to the industrial injury.
32.Claimant proved it is more probably true than not the April 8, 2025 industrial
injury caused a disability lasting more three work shifts, she left work as a result
of the disability, and the disability resulted in an actual wage loss from April 9,
2025, ongoing. Claimant is entitled to TTD benefits from April 9, 2025, ongoing.
Conclusions of Law
Generally
A. The purpose of the Workers’ Compensation Act of Colorado, §§ 8-40-101, et
seq., C.R.S. is to assure the quick and efficient delivery of disability and medical
benefits to injured workers at a reasonable cost to employers, without the
necessity of litigation. See § 8-40-102(1), C.R.S. Claimant shoulders the burden
of proving entitlement to benefits by a preponderance of the evidence. See § 8-
10

43-201, C.R.S. A preponderance of the evidence is that which leads the trier-of-
fact, after considering all of the evidence, to find that a fact is more probably true
than not. Page v. Clark, 592 P.2d 792 (Colo. 1979). The facts in a workers’
compensation case must be interpreted neutrally; neither in favor of the rights of
the claimant, nor in favor of the rights of respondents; and a workers’
compensation claim shall be decided on the merits. § 8-43-201, C.R.S.
B. Assessing weight, credibility, and sufficiency of evidence in Workers'
Compensation proceedings is the exclusive domain of the administrative law
judge. University Park Care Center v. Indus. Claim Appeals Office, 43 P.3d 637
(Colo. App. 2001). Even if other evidence in the record may have supported a
contrary inference, it is for the ALJ to resolve conflicts in the evidence, make
credibility determinations, and draw plausible inferences from the evidence. Id. at
641. When determining credibility, the fact finder should consider, among other
things, the consistency or inconsistency of the witness's testimony and actions;
the reasonableness or unreasonableness (probability or improbability) of the
testimony and actions; the motives of the witness; whether the testimony has
been contradicted; and bias, prejudice, or interest. Prudential Ins. Co. v. Cline, 57
P.2d 1205 (Colo. 1936); Bodensieck v. Indus. Claim Appeals Office, 183 P.3d
684 (Colo. App. 2008). The weight and credibility to be assigned expert
testimony is a matter within the discretion of the ALJ. Cordova v. Indus. Claim
Appeals Office, 55 P.3d 186 (Colo. App. 2002). To the extent expert testimony is
subject to conflicting interpretations, the ALJ may resolve the conflict by crediting
part or none of the testimony. Colorado Springs Motors, Ltd. v. Indus. Comm’n,
441 P.2d 21 (Colo. 1968).
C. The ALJ's factual findings concern only evidence and inferences found to be
dispositive of the issues involved; the ALJ has not addressed every piece of
evidence or every inference that might lead to conflicting conclusions and has
rejected evidence contrary to the above findings as unpersuasive. Magnetic
Eng’g, Inc. v. Indus. Claim Appeals Office, 5 P.3d 385 (Colo. App. 2000).
11

Compensability
D. To establish a compensable injury an employee must prove by a preponderance
of the evidence that his injury arose out of the course and scope of employment
with his employer. §8-41-301(1)(b), C.R.S. (2006); see City of Boulder v. Streeb,
706 P.2d 786, 791 (Colo. 1985). An injury occurs "in the course of" employment
when a claimant demonstrates that the injury occurred within the time and place
limits of his employment and during an activity that had some connection with his
work-related functions. Triad Painting Co. v. Blair, 812 P.2d 638, 641 (Colo.
1991). The "arising out of" requirement is narrower and requires the claimant to
demonstrate that the injury has its “origin in an employee's work-related functions
and is sufficiently related thereto to be considered part of the employee’s service
to the employer.” Popovich v. Irlando, 811 P.2d 379, 383 (Colo. 1991). The
claimant must prove a causal nexus between the claimed disability and the work-
related injury. Singleton v. Kenya Corp., 961 P.2d 571 (Colo. App. 1998).
E. A pre-existing condition does not disqualify a claim if the employment
aggravates, accelerates, or combines with the pre-existing disease to produce a
disability or need for medical treatment. Duncan v. Indus. Claim Appeals Off.,
107 P.3d 999 (Colo. App. 2004); Enriquez v. Americold D/B/A Atlas Logistics,
WC 4-960-513-01, (ICAO, Oct. 2, 2015). The industrial injury need not be the
sole cause of the disability if the injury is a significant, direct, and consequential
factor in the disability. See Subsequent Injury Fund v. Indus. Claim Appeals Off.,
131 P.3d 1224 (Colo. App. 2006); Joslins Dry Goods Co. v. Indus. Claim Appeals
Off., 21 P.3d 866 (Colo. App. 2001).
F. Pain is a typical symptom from the aggravation of a pre-existing condition. See
Merriman v. Indus. Comm’n, 120 Colo. 400, 210 P.2d 448 (1949). However, the
mere experience of symptoms at work does not necessarily require a finding that
the employment aggravated or accelerated the pre-existing condition. Resolution
of that issue is also one of fact for the ALJ. F.R. Orr Construction v. Rinta, 717
P.2d 965 (Colo. App. 1985). Temporal proximity should not be mistaken for a
12

causal relationship and correlation is not causation. See Scully v. Hooters of
Colorado Springs, W.C. No. 4-745-712 (ICAO, Oct. 27, 2008). When a claimant
experiences symptoms while at work it is for the ALJ to determine whether the
subsequent need for treatment was caused by an industrial aggravation of a pre-
existing condition or by the natural progression of the pre-existing condition. In re
Shaffstall, W.C. No. 4-820-016 (ICAO, Mar. 2, 2011).
G. As found, Claimant proved it is more probably true than not she suffered a
compensable industrial injury on April 8, 2025. While Dr. Koenig emphasizes
that Claimant provided different descriptions of the mechanism of injury, the
record demonstrates Claimant has overall consistently reported the same
mechanism of injury – experiencing a pop and immediate pain while throwing a
strap to secure a load – to providers in the days immediately following the injury
and thereafter. Claimant was unable to complete her shift on April 8, 2025 as a
result of the injury. It is undisputed that Claimant has a history of prior right
shoulder pain and treatment. Nonetheless, Claimant credibly and persuasively
testified, and there is no evidence to the contrary, that such symptoms required
consistent treatment or impaired Claimant’s ability to perform her regular job
duties prior to the work injury. Despite right shoulder pain dating back to 2019,
the records demonstrate Claimant sought treatment for such symptoms
approximately every 1.5 years, the symptoms were adequately managed by
steroid injections, and Claimant remained able to perform her regular job duties.
While Claimant experienced right shoulder pain in the two months leading up to
the work injury, such symptoms did not cause Claimant to seek medical
treatment at the time nor did they impair her ability to perform her regular work.
H. On April 8, 2025, while performing her regular job duties during her regular work
shift, Claimant experienced an immediate pop and pain in her right shoulder,
which she credibly testified and consistently reported was different and and
worse than her prior pain. The injury resulted in Claimant being placed on work
restrictions and the need for medical treatment, including physical therapy and
13

surgery. The ALJ found the opinions of Drs. Walker and Caldwell and NP
Schubert more credible and persuasive than the opinions of Drs. Hattem and
Koenig. As documented in their records, Dr. Walker, Dr. Caldwell, and NP
Schubert were aware of Claimant’s prior right shoulder pain leading up to the
work injury and nevertheless credibly opined that Claimant sustained a work-
related exacerbation of her chronic degenerative condition. Based on the totality
of the credible and persuasive evidence, Claimant has met her burden to prove
she suffered an injury arising out of and in the course and scope of her
employment that caused disability and the need for medical treatment.
Medical Benefits
I. Respondents are liable for medical treatment that is reasonable and necessary to
cure and relieve the effects of the industrial injury. §8-42-101(1)(a), C.R.S. The
question of whether the claimant proved treatment is reasonable and necessary
is one of fact for the ALJ. Kroupa v. Indus. Claim Appeals Off., 53 P.3d 1192
(Colo. App. 2002). Hobirk v. Colorado Springs School Dist. #11, WC 4-835-556-
01 (ICAO, Nov. 15, 2012). For a service to be considered a “medical benefit” it
must be provided as medical or nursing treatment or incidental to obtaining such
treatment. Country Squires Kennels v. Tarshis, 899 P.2d 362 (Colo. App. 1995).
A service is medically necessary if it cures or relieves the effects of the injury and
is directly associated with the claimant’s physical needs. Bellone v. Indus. Claim
Appeals Off., 940 P.2d 1116 (Colo. App. 1997); Parker v. Iowa Tanklines, Inc.,
WC 4-517-537 (ICAO, May 31, 2006).
J. As Claimant proved she sustained a compensable work injury, Respondents are
liable for reasonably necessary and related treatment to relieve the effects of the
industrial injury. As found, Claimant proved it is more probably true than not the
treatment she received for her right shoulder, including the right total shoulder
arthroplasty, was causally related to the April 8, 2025 work injury and reasonable
and necessary to cure and relieve its effects. As discussed above, despite
Claimant’s pre-existing chronic shoulder condition, Claimant was treating with
14

injections, not seeking consistent or frequent treatment, and was able to perform
her regular job duties. There is no evidence in the record a recommendation for a
reverse total shoulder arthroplasty had been made prior to the work injury, or to
otherwise suggest when Claimant would have required such surgery absent the
industrial injury. Despite some reported improvement in pain and function
documented in the physical therapy records, Claimant credibly testified that she
had not returned to her “baseline” prior to the surgery. Claimant also remained on
work restrictions at such time. While it is clear Claimant had a pre-existing
chronic degenerative condition, the totality of the credible and persuasive
evidence demonstrates the industrial injury aggravated the pre-existing condition
producing the need for the medical treatment, including the surgery as
recommended by Dr. Caldwell. Dr. Caldwell’s opinion as to the reasonableness,
necessity and relatedness of the surgery is more persuasive than those of Drs.
Hattem and Koenig, who opine there was no work-related injury. Accordingly,
Respondents are liable for the costs of the reverse total shoulder arthroplasty, as
well as other reasonably necessary and causally related medical treatment.
Temporary Total Disability Benefits
K. To prove entitlement to TTD benefits, a claimant must prove that the industrial
injury caused a disability lasting more than three work shifts, he left work as a
result of the disability, and the disability resulted in an actual wage loss. See §§8-
42-(1)(g) & 8-42-105(4), C.R.S.; Anderson v. Longmont Toyota, 102 P.3d 323
(Colo. 2004); City of Colorado Springs v. Indus. Claim Appeals Off., 954 P.2d
637 (Colo. App. 1997). Section 8-42-103(1)(a), C.R.S. requires the claimant to
establish a causal connection between a work-related injury and a subsequent
wage loss in order to obtain TTD benefits. The term “disability” connotes two
elements: (1) medical incapacity evidenced by loss or restriction of bodily
function; and (2) impairment of wage earning capacity as demonstrated by
claimant's inability to resume his or her prior work. Culver v. Ace Electric, 971
P.2d 641, 649 (Colo. 1999). The impairment of earning capacity element of
15

disability may be evidenced by a complete inability to work or by restrictions
which impair the claimant's ability effectively and properly to perform his or her
regular employment. Ortiz v. Charles J. Murphy & Co., 964 P.2d 595, 597 (Colo.
App. 1998). Because there is no requirement that a claimant must produce
evidence of medical restrictions, a claimant’s testimony alone is sufficient to
demonstrate a disability. Lymburn v. Symbios Logic, 952 P.2d 831, 833 (Colo.
App. 1997).
L. TTD benefits shall continue until the first occurrence of any of the following: (1)
the employee reaches MMI; (2) the employee returns to regular or modified
employment; (3) the attending physician gives the employee a written release to
return to regular employment; or (4) the attending physician gives the employee
a written release to return to modified employment, the employment is offered in
writing and the employee fails to begin the employment. §8-42-105(3)(a)-(d),
C.R.S.; see Chavez v. Costco Wholesale, Inc., WC 5-096-055-003 (ICAO, Feb.
4, 2022) (noting that, where TTD benefits had not commenced, they could not be
terminated based on the ATP’s MMI determination).
M. As found, Claimant proved it is more probable than not she is entitled to TTD
benefits from April 9, 2025 ongoing. As a result of the April 9, 2025 industrial
injury to her right shoulder, Claimant was placed on work restrictions and unable
to effectively and properly perform her regular job duties. Claimant has remained
on work restrictions impairing her ability to return to her regular employment, has
not been offered modified employment, nor has she been placed at MMI. As a
result of the April 9, 2025 industrial injury and resultant disability, Claimant has
not earned any wages from April 9, 2025 ongoing, entitling her to TTD benefits
for such time period.
Order
It is therefore ordered that:

1. Claimant sustained a compensable industrial injury on April 8, 2025 arising out of
and in the course and scope of her employment.
2. Claimant is entitled to reasonable, necessary and related medical benefits to
cure and relieve the effects of her April 8, 2025 work injury. The treatment
Claimant received for her right shoulder, including the reverse total right shoulder
arthroplasty, was reasonable, necessary, and related to her April 8, 2025 work
injury. Respondents shall pay for the associated costs of such treatment, as well
as other reasonable, necessary and related medical treatment, subject to the
Division of Workers’ Compensation Fee Schedule.
3. Respondent shall pay Claimant TTD benefits from April 9, 2025, ongoing until
terminated by law.
4. Claimant’s AWW is $752.77, with a corresponding TTD rate $501.85.
5. Respondents shall pay interest at the rate of 8% per annum on all benefits,
including TTD, not paid when due.
6. All matters not determined herein are reserved for future determination.
